title: India Orders Wind Turbine Makers to Store All Data Locally Amid Rising Cyberattack Threats
excerpt: The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy mandates data localisation, domestic operational control, and in-country R&D centres for all ALMM-listed wind turbine manufacturers.
body:
• India's Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has ordered all wind turbine manufacturers on the ALMM list to report their cybersecurity compliance status by month's end.
  • New rules mandate that all wind turbine operational data be stored in India, with no real-time data transfers outside the country and operational control exclusively from within India.
  • Foreign manufacturers must establish R&D centres in India within one year of the July 31, 2025 deadline set in the draft amendment.
  • The directive follows growing global concern over energy infrastructure cyberattacks, including Iran's August 2026 attack on a UK power plant that shut operations for four days.

MNRE Orders Cybersecurity Compliance Reports

India's Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) has directed all wind turbine manufacturers listed on the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) to submit cybersecurity compliance status reports by the end of August 2026. The order enforces requirements first outlined in a draft amendment dated April 17, 2025, which mandated data localisation and operational security controls for wind energy infrastructure connected to India's power grid.

The compliance requirements are sweeping: all data centres and servers handling wind turbine data must be located in India, all operational data must be stored domestically, no real-time operational data may be transferred outside the country, and operational control must be exercised exclusively from within India, MediaNama reported.

Foreign Manufacturers Face R&D Mandate

In addition to the data localisation requirements, foreign wind turbine manufacturers on the ALMM list must set up research and development centres in India within one year from July 31, 2025. The provision pushes international turbine makers — many of whom have significant operations in India — to deepen their domestic presence beyond manufacturing and sales.

The requirement is likely to affect major global players such as Vestas, Siemens Gamesa, and Envision, though the MNRE order does not name specific companies. For Indian-origin engineers working at these multinationals, the mandate could create new R&D opportunities in India.

Cyberattack Threats Drive Urgency

The timing of the MNRE directive is not coincidental. On August 24, 2026, Iran launched a cyberattack against a UK power plant that forced a four-day shutdown — a stark demonstration of how vulnerable energy infrastructure has become to state-sponsored hacking. Estonia's experience with Russian cyberattacks in 2007 remains another frequently cited precedent for infrastructure-targeted digital warfare.

"Wind turbines connected to the national and state grid can be compromised remotely, posing risks to energy security."

— NITI Aayog, 2024 report on renewable energy cybersecurity

A 2024 NITI Aayog report specifically flagged cybersecurity risks posed by wind turbines connected to electricity grids, warning about Power Plant Controllers of foreign origin — particularly those from "neighbouring countries," a veiled reference to Chinese-manufactured components that are widely deployed in India's wind energy sector.

Data Localisation Without a National Mandate

India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act does not impose a blanket data localisation requirement. However, sectoral regulators have increasingly pushed localisation rules within their domains. The Reserve Bank of India mandated financial data localisation in 2018, and the MNRE's wind turbine directive follows the same pattern — sector-specific rules filling gaps left by the national framework.

The approach reflects a pragmatic calculation: critical infrastructure data, particularly data that could be used to disrupt power grids, carries risks that general-purpose data protection rules are not designed to address. The MNRE's focus on preventing real-time operational data transfers suggests specific concern about foreign actors monitoring or manipulating turbine performance in real time.

What's Next

Manufacturers have until the end of August to submit their compliance reports. Non-compliant companies risk removal from the ALMM list, which would effectively bar them from supplying turbines to Indian projects that receive government subsidies or participate in public tenders. The enforcement timeline for the R&D centre requirement extends to mid-2026, giving foreign manufacturers roughly a year from the original draft amendment to establish physical research operations in India.

As India pushes toward its target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel power capacity by 2030, the tension between rapid renewable deployment and infrastructure security will only sharpen. The MNRE's directive signals that New Delhi is unwilling to trade energy security for speed.
